text: Viruses are very small microorganisms, too small to see with a normal microscope, and cannot grow or reproduce outside of animal cells. A virus invades living cells and hijacks their chemical machinery to stay alive and replicate, often damaging or destroying the infected cells. Viruses can reproduce with copying errors called mutations, which is part of why vaccination is not always fully effective against some diseases like PRRS. Outside the animal body, viruses cannot replicate and are inert, but can still survive for months in the environment — for example Newcastle Disease Virus can survive several weeks in a warm, humid environment on feathers, manure, and other materials. Some viruses multiply in an animal without causing symptoms — ducks with Bird Flu can look healthy while shedding large amounts of virus, even though chickens are highly sensitive and will die if contaminated; the severity of disease from the same virus can vary by species. Clinical signs depend on which organ the virus attacks — for example in Classical Swine Fever (CSF) the virus damages small blood vessel cells, causing small hemorrhages in organs or skin. Antibiotics are not effective against viruses.
